consensus_summary: Night primarily symbolizes spiritual darkness, the realm of sin, evil, unbelief, and separation from God, standing in contrast to day/light as God, Christ, truth, and salvation; believers are children of the day, and the new creation has no night.
book_summary: Night is the time of darkness—hiding and sleep, when opportunity closes; the children of the night sleep and are drunken, doing their deeds in the dark.
consensus_core_identification: spiritual darkness / sin / evil / unbelief / separation from God (contrasted with day/light)
book_core_identification: time of darkness marked by hiding, sleep, closed opportunity, and the sleep/drunkenness/dark deeds of the children of the night
boundary_disagreement: None; book's concrete descriptors (hiding, sleep, drunkenness, deeds in dark, opportunity closing) are drawn from the same primary texts without excluding or reclassifying the consensus applications of spiritual darkness.
rationale: Minimum cores are equivalent: both identify night with the spiritual/moral darkness of sin and unbelief via the identical key texts (especially 1 Thess 5:5-7 and the day/night dualism). Book's phrasing supplies applicative detail and near-paraphrase from those texts rather than altering the referent, narrowing/broadening the category, or introducing contradiction; extra particulars do not create artificial disagreement.
strongest_objection: The book foregrounds 'opportunity closes' and behavioral particulars (hiding/sleep/drunkenness), which could be read as tilting toward the 'end of opportunity' alternative rather than pure ontological darkness, but this remains inside the consensus primary and its common supporting texts.
